sections.skill: Apply the rules for withdrawing Roth IRA contributions and earnings

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Mia, 30, made $8,000 of regular contributions to her Roth IRA over several years, with no conversions, rollovers, or earlier withdrawals. It is worth $11,000. She withdraws $5,000. Under the ordering rules, what is taxed or penalized?

choices.text: Only the 10% additional tax, which would be $500

questions.intro: Roth IRA withdrawals come out in a set order: regular contributions first, then conversion and rollover amounts (which have their own rules), then earnings. Regular contributions were made with after-tax money, so they can be withdrawn at any time, at any age, without tax or penalty.
questions.feedback: Her first $8,000 withdrawn counts as regular contributions, so $5,000 is tax- and penalty-free.
questions.topic: Roth IRA withdrawals and qualified distributions

misconceptions.A: Thinks every early withdrawal is taxed

sources: IRS (Publication 590-B): Roth IRA regular contributions can be withdrawn at any time; distributions come out in order: regular contributions, then conversions and rollovers, then earnings; qualified distributions need a 5-year period and age 59½ (or death, disability, or a first-time home purchase up to $10,000); nonqualified earnings may be taxed plus a 10% additional tax. (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590b)
IRS (Publication 590-A): One annual contribution limit covers all of a person's traditional and Roth IRAs combined. (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p590a)

questions.prompt: Mia later withdraws $2,000 of EARNINGS at age 32, and no exception applies. Assume her tax rate is 12%. How much tax and additional tax is due?
questions.intro: Earnings withdrawn before a "qualified distribution" are generally taxable as income, and before age 59½ they usually also face a 10% additional tax, unless an exception applies.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Which conditions make a Roth IRA distribution QUALIFIED (tax-free, including earnings)?

choices.text: Any withdrawal after the account is one year old
Five years since the first Roth contribution AND age 59½ (or another qualifying event)
Any withdrawal at all, because Roth means tax-free

questions.correct_answer: Five years since the first Roth contribution AND age 59½ (or another qualifying event)
questions.intro: A qualified Roth distribution meets two tests: the 5-year rule (5 tax years since your first Roth IRA contribution) and a qualifying event: age 59½, disability, death, or a first-time home purchase (up to $10,000 lifetime).
questions.feedback: Both the 5-year period and a qualifying event (usually age 59½) are required.

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Leo opens his first Roth IRA at age 58 with a contribution for tax year 2026. At what point does he first meet BOTH tests for qualified distributions?

choices.text: Immediately, because he is already over age 55 and retired
In 2031, when 5 years have passed and he is over 59½

questions.correct_answer: In 2031, when 5 years have passed and he is over 59½
questions.intro: The 5-year clock starts January 1 of the tax year of the first Roth IRA contribution.
questions.feedback: The clock starts January 1, 2026; five years later is January 1, 2031, when he is already over 59½.

questions.prompt: Which IRA type requires minimum withdrawals starting in the owner's 70s?
questions.intro: Required minimum distributions (RMDs) are yearly withdrawals the IRS requires so that tax-deferred money is eventually taxed. They start in an owner's 70s, depending on birth year. Money taxed before it went in is treated differently.
questions.feedback: Traditional IRAs have RMDs; Roth IRAs do not for the original owner.

choices.text: "A Roth IRA is an account that holds investments."

questions.domain: Retirement Accounts: IRAs, Roth IRAs, 401(k)s, and 403(b)s
questions.prompt: Sam is single and has no spouse's income to use. He contributed $6,000 to a Roth IRA this year but earned only $2,500. What mistake occurred?

choices.text: He contributed more than his compensation
None; contributions are not limited by income
He should have contributed more to reach the full limit
He contributed in the wrong tax year

questions.correct_answer: He contributed more than his compensation
questions.intro: Total IRA contributions for a year cannot exceed your taxable compensation (except spousal IRAs on a joint return).
questions.feedback: $6,000 − $2,500 = $3,500 excess, subject to a 6% tax for each year it stays uncorrected.
